text:
Yes. There can be duties to oneself, and a person can wrong themselves even when no one else is harmed.

My position is that morality is not only about preventing harm to other people; it is also about how one treats rational agency, character, and the human good in one’s own life. If that is right, then self-directed destruction, degradation, or neglect can be morally wrong even when it has no direct victims besides the agent.

A simple way to see this is to ask what makes something morally significant. If the answer is “the value of persons,” then that value does not disappear when the person in question is oneself. If I matter morally when you deal with me, I also matter morally when I deal with myself. To say otherwise would be odd: it would mean I must not lie to you, humiliate you, or needlessly injure you because you have dignity, but I may freely humiliate or destroy myself because the same dignity somehow vanishes in the first-person case. That seems unstable. The dignity of a person is not dependent on who is acting.

This idea is strongest in a Kantian form. On that view, each person has a duty to respect rational nature, including in themselves. That means not treating oneself as a mere tool for appetite, convenience, or escape. Some forms of self-harm are wrong not because they produce social costs, but because they express a failure of respect for one’s own status as an end in oneself. If someone deliberately wrecks their mind, squanders their capacities, or reduces themselves to an object of use, they may violate a duty of self-respect.

There is also an Aristotelian version of the same thought. Ethics is about flourishing: becoming the kind of person who lives well as a human being. On that picture, cowardice, self-indulgence, sloth, and self-mutilation are not wrong only because they affect others; they are defects in one’s own life. A person can fail at living well. Even in total isolation, someone can become vicious, disordered, and alienated from their own good. That is a moral failure, not merely a prudential mistake.

Someone might object that this collapses morality into paternalism. If I am the only one affected, why not say I am merely being unwise, not immoral? This is a serious objection, because not every self-regarding mistake should be moralized. Eating badly for a week, wasting a weekend, taking a nonlethal risk for excitement, or choosing an unconventional life is not automatically a violation of duty. Adults need room for autonomy, experimentation, even folly. A duty to oneself should not become a license for moral busybodies.

But that objection shows only that the category must be used carefully, not that it is empty. There is a difference between choices that merely depart from optimization and choices that amount to self-betrayal. Recklessness, addiction, cruelty toward oneself, and the deliberate abandonment of one’s basic capacities can cross that line. The wrongness lies in the will’s stance toward the self: contempt, refusal of responsibility, or surrender of agency.

Another objection is that if a person freely chooses self-harm, then autonomy itself justifies the act. But autonomy is not the same as permission to annihilate the conditions that make agency possible. Freedom is valuable partly because it lets us pursue goods, form commitments, and shape a life. When it is used to dismantle the very capacities that make meaningful choice possible, that can be a misuse of freedom rather than its highest expression.

Still, this moral wrong is distinctive. If I wrong myself, the wrong does not automatically authorize other people to coerce me. That is an important distinction. Something can be morally criticizable without being properly punishable. We often have reasons to preserve liberty even when people choose badly. So affirming duties to oneself does not require legal paternalism or social intrusion into every private vice.

In short: yes, there is such a thing as a duty to oneself. A person with no dependents can still do wrong by degrading, damaging, or failing to respect their own humanity. Morality concerns not only what we owe others, but also what we owe the person each of us unavoidably governs: ourselves.
